title: Define the Ferox FP profile so it strengthens regularity and safety without increasing semantic entropy
description: Evaluate how far Ferox should lean into FP ideas such as ADTs, exhaustive matching, expression-oriented code, immutability-by-default, pipelines, and pure helper functions. The goal is to identify which FP influences strengthen Ferox's core thesis around safe change, low entropy, and agent-friendly tooling, and which FP directions would harm compile times, local reasoning, or systems-language coherence.
design: Current working hypothesis: restrained FP helps Ferox when it improves source-code regularity and local reasoning, but harms Ferox when it introduces major new semantic machinery. Likely good fits include ADTs, exhaustive matching, expression orientation, immutable-by-default style, and a narrow pipe operator. Likely bad fits include effect-heavy purity systems, monadic abstraction culture, operator proliferation, higher-kinded types, lazy defaults, and multiple equivalent composition idioms.
acceptance_criteria: Produce a clear Ferox FP doctrine that explains: 1. which FP ideas are core to the language identity; 2. which are useful but secondary; 3. which are out of scope because they would widen the core too much; 4. how the recommended FP profile interacts with ownership, async, tooling, compile times, and future verification.

title: Define the new Ferox vision around safe change: low-entropy systems design, FP-shaped readability, fast feedback, and verification-ready tooling
description: Refine the Ferox vision into a sharper and more defensible thesis. The current direction under discussion is an ownership-based systems language for safe change: Rust-grade safe-code guarantees, lower semantic entropy than Rust, explicit performance behavior, FP-shaped readability, fast incremental feedback, and tooling designed for humans and agents to evolve large codebases without semantic drift.
design: Target shape: ADTs, exhaustive matching, expression-oriented code, immutable-by-default data flow, and a narrow pipe style inspired by the best parts of Gleam and Elixir, but without runtime magic or effect-heavy complexity. Keep ownership, mutation, async, and sharing explicit. Avoid syntax macros, trait/generic sprawl, and capability-heavy concurrency in the near term. Strengthen the tooling story around query-native incremental compilation, full-fidelity syntax trees, canonical formatting, structured diagnostics, normalized checked IR, and a first-party structural rule/autofix system. Treat verification as a later optional layer built around contracts, ghost/spec code, and proof-oriented tooling for critical modules rather than as a proof-first core language. Current version framing under discussion: v1 = Safe Core, v2 = Safe Change, v3 = Deep Assurance.
acceptance_criteria: A revised Ferox vision should clearly explain: 1. why Ferox exists if Rust already delivers strong safety; 2. what 'better for agents' means mechanically; 3. how FP influence improves readability without increasing entropy; 4. why fast feedback and incremental checking are core product requirements; 5. which high-leverage external ideas genuinely strengthen Ferox; 6. which ideas remain out of scope because they would widen the core too much; 7. how simple staged descriptions for v1, v2, and v3 follow from the thesis rather than feeling like unrelated feature buckets.
notes: The vision cleanup pass is now complete in principle: the accepted direction has been folded into the canonical docs, and the temporary draft vision files were removed to leave one primary vision set. .beads/.gitignore was also updated to ignore .br_history tracker artifacts produced by br.
